usage: It's so frustrating I could die
examples: It's frustrating because we can't communicate.
-아서/어서 ties cause to feeling; 통하다 = get through
설명을 해도 못 알아들으니까 진짜 답답해요.
Even when I explain, they don't get it, so I'm really frustrated.
nuance: 답답하다 spans two worlds with one word: a physical airless, closed-in feeling (a small windowless room, a stuffy nose, a tight chest) and an emotional one — being penned-in frustrated when a situation won't budge or you cannot make yourself understood. The dividing line from 화나다 (angry) is direction: 화나다 explodes outward at a target, while 답답하다 is the smothered, helpless 'I can't breathe / can't fix this' pressure that turns inward; 짜증나다 (irritated) is sharper and more peevish. It is a 하다 adjective, so 답답하 + 아요 fuses to 답답해요 (never 답답하요). It loves the subjects 가슴/속/마음 (chest/stomach/heart) and the phrase 말이 안 통하다. English-speaker pitfall: do not translate 'I'm frustrated WITH you' word-for-word with an object particle — 답답하다 describes the speaker's own stifled state, so you say 답답해요, and if you must name the cause you append it with -아서/어서, not with 을/를.

mistakes: Conjugating as 답답하요; 하다 adjectives fuse 하+아 into 해, giving 답답해요.
Using it to mean 'angry at someone' — 답답하다 is the stifled, helpless feeling; for outward anger use 화나다.
Attaching a person with 을/를 (사람을 답답해요 ✗); state the cause with -아서/어서 instead: 말이 안 통해서 답답해요.

usage: I ate until I was full
I'm so full I could burst
examples: I ate a lot, so I'm full.
I only ate a little but I'm already full.
다 못 먹겠어요. 너무 배불러서 숟가락도 못 들겠어요.
I can't finish it. I'm so full I can't even lift my spoon.
nuance: 배부르다 literally welds 배 (belly) + 부르다 here meaning 'swollen/filled', and names the satisfied, can't-eat-more fullness after a meal — the exact opposite of 배고프다 (hungry). Mind the boundary: 배부르다 is a finished state ('I AM full'), whereas the verb 부르다/불렀다 describes the belly filling up, and 질리다 means 'sick of / fed up with' a food rather than physically full. It is a 르-irregular adjective: when an ending starting with 아/어 attaches, the 르 drops its ㅡ and doubles the ㄹ, so 배부르 + 어요 → 배불러요 (past 배불렀어요). Socially it doubles as a polite signal that you enjoyed the meal and are content — saying 잘 먹었어요. 배불러요 graciously declines a second helping. English-speaker pitfall: 'I'm full' is a whole-body sentence in English, but Korean keeps the belly in view, so the natural line is just 배불러요, not 저는 가득해요 (a 직역 of 'full' that sounds like a filled container).

usage: 하나도 + negative = not in the least
examples: I had high hopes, but the movie was boring.
Playing alone is no fun, so let's play together.
nuance: 재미없다 is the fixed antonym of 재미있다 (fun/interesting), built from the noun 재미 (fun/enjoyment) + 없다 (there isn't) and written solid as one word. It judges whether an activity or media delivers enjoyment — a film, game, class, party, person's stories. Distinguish it from 심심하다, which describes YOUR own state of having nothing to do ('I'm bored'), and from 지루하다, which stresses tedious, drags-on dullness; 재미없다 is the verdict on the THING ('it's not fun'). Crucial structure point: 없다 already carries the negative, so you never stack 안 in front of it (안 재미없어요 ✗). To flip it positive you must swap the whole word to 재미있어요, not negate this one. English-speaker pitfall: learners try to say 'I'm not having fun' by negating the adjective, but Korean assigns the quality to the event, so you say 이거 재미없어요 ('this is boring'), and the spacing trap 재미 없어요 (two words) reads as raw 'there is no fun' rather than the dictionary headword.

usage: I ate it even though it wasn't tasty
examples: simple verdict on food; topic + 맛없어요
It tastes bad because it got cold.
맛없으면 억지로 먹지 말고 남겨도 돼요.
If it's bad, don't force it down — you can leave it.
nuance: 맛없다 is the straight antonym of 맛있다 (delicious), welded from the noun 맛 (taste) + 없다 (there isn't), written as one word. It is a blunt taste verdict, so soften it in company with 좀 (좀 맛없어요, 'it's a bit off') rather than declaring it flatly to a host. Watch the pronunciation: the final ㅅ of 맛 resyllabifies and tenses into the next syllable, so 맛없어요 is said [마덥써요], not letter-by-letter [맏업어요]. As with 재미없다, the 없다 already supplies the negative, so 안 맛없어요 is wrong — to flip it positive you change the whole word to 맛있어요. English-speaker pitfall: 'this is not tasty' tempts learners to negate with 안, but Korean treats 맛없다 as its own lexical antonym; also note 맛없다 means literally tasteless/bad, while 별로예요 ('it's not great / so-so') is the gentler, more common dodge Koreans use to avoid bluntly insulting someone's cooking.

examples: The subway is more convenient than the bus.
집에 오니까 마음이 편해서 잠이 잘 와요.
Now that I'm home I feel at ease, so I sleep well.
nuance: 편하다 carries the Sino-Korean root 便 (편, 'convenient / at ease') and stretches across three senses English splits into separate words: physical comfort (a comfy chair, loose clothes), practical convenience (handy transport, an easy method), and inner ease (a relaxed, untroubled mind, 마음이 편하다). It is the antonym of 불편하다. Mind two boundaries: 쉽다 means 'easy to DO' a task (the problem is simple), whereas 편하다 means 'comfortable/convenient' (low effort or strain) — a method can be 쉽다 yet not 편하다; and 편안하다 is the softer, more soothing 'peaceful/at rest' cousin you meet in 편안한 밤 (a restful night). As a 하다 adjective it becomes 편해요, and the adverb 편하게 powers warm invitations like 편하게 드세요 / 편하게 계세요 ('help yourself / make yourself at home'). English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 편하다 to translate 'easy' on a test — 시험이 편했어요 sounds like the exam was low-strain, not 'the questions were easy'; for that you want 쉬웠어요.

usage: I feel unwell / my body is impaired
polite way to say unwell or disabled
a point of inconvenience / a complaint
examples: 여기는 교통이 불편해서 차가 꼭 필요해요.
Transit here is inconvenient, so you really need a car.
처음 만난 사람이랑 단둘이 있으면 좀 불편해요.
Being alone with someone I just met feels a bit awkward.
nuance: 불편하다 fronts the Sino-Korean negative prefix 不 (불, 'not') onto 便 (편, 'convenient'), literally 'not-convenient', and is the all-purpose antonym of 편하다. It covers physical discomfort (tight shoes, a hard bed), practical inconvenience (poor transport, a clunky process), social unease (feeling awkward around someone), and gently, being unwell or physically impaired (몸이 불편하다 is the courteous phrase for illness or disability). It is the polite backbone of complaints — service desks ask 불편한 점이 있으셨어요? ('was anything inconvenient?'). Boundary note: 불편하다 is the broad 'uncomfortable/inconvenient', while 어색하다 zeroes in on the awkward unfamiliarity between people who aren't close, and 아프다 is plain physical pain. As a 하다 adjective it conjugates to 불편해요. English-speaker pitfall: the literal calque 안 편하다 is understood but sounds like a learner workaround — the natural single lexical antonym is 불편하다; and don't use 불편하다 for sharp pain, which is 아파요.

usage: 속상해하다 = to act/show upset, comforting someone
I'm so upset I could die
examples: I'm upset because I did badly on the test.
I worked hard on it but ruined it all, so I'm gutted.
아이가 아픈데 해 줄 게 없어서 너무 속상해요.
My child is sick and there's nothing I can do, so it breaks my heart.
nuance: 속상하다 literally pairs 속 (one's insides / heart) with 상하다, which uses the hanja 傷 (상, 'to wound, spoil') — so the image is your insides getting bruised. It is the warm everyday word for being upset, gutted, or heart-sore over a letdown, a hurtful word, or something that goes wrong, and Koreans apply it to small daily disappointments as readily as bigger hurts. Mark the boundaries carefully: 화나다 is hot anger aimed outward, 슬프다 is plain sadness (a sad film, a loss), while 속상하다 sits in between as a tender, often self-directed 'this hurts / I'm so disappointed' ache, frequently mixed with helplessness. Grammar trap unique to feeling-adjectives: for your OWN feeling say 속상해요, but to describe someone ELSE's visible upset you must add 하 → 친구가 속상해해요 ('my friend is upset'), because Korean treats another person's inner emotion as something you observe, not assert. English-speaker pitfall: don't substitute 화나다 for every 'upset' — in English 'upset' often means hurt/disappointed, which is exactly 속상하다, whereas 화나다 means genuinely angry.

usage: The sole of my foot is ticklish
examples: simple: common pre-cough sensation, body part + 이
When you touch my armpit it tickles.
새 스웨터가 목에 닿아서 간지러워 죽겠어요.
The new sweater touches my neck and it's unbearably itchy.
nuance: 간지럽다 covers two related skin sensations: the squirmy tickle when someone touches a ticklish spot, and a light, fluttery itch on the skin or throat (the kind that makes you clear your throat). It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective, so before an 어 ending the ㅂ turns into 우 and merges: 간지럽 + 어요 → 간지러워요 (past 간지러웠어요). The key contrast is intensity and intent: 간지럽다 is the lighter, ticklish/mildly-itchy feeling, whereas 가렵다 is the stronger 'must-scratch' itch (a mosquito bite, a rash). English-speaker pitfall: English uses 'itchy' for both, but Korean splits them, so a serious itch you'd scratch hard is 가려워요, not 간지러워요. Also, mark the body part with the subject particle 이/가 (등이 간지러워요, 'my back is itchy'), never the object particle 을/를 — the back is what HAS the sensation, not something being acted on.

examples: We just met today, so it's a bit awkward.
오랜만에 봐서 그런지 둘이 좀 어색해요.
Maybe because it's been a while, the two of them seem a bit awkward.
머리를 자르니까 거울 속 내가 어색해 보여요.
After the haircut, the me in the mirror looks unfamiliar/odd.
nuance: 어색하다 traces to the Sino-Korean 語塞 (어 語 'speech' + 색 塞 'blocked/stuck') — the picture of words getting jammed — and names two feelings: the stiff, uneasy awkwardness between people who aren't yet close, and the sense that something looks or feels unnatural or out of place (a forced smile, a new haircut, an odd-sounding sentence). It is the antonym of 자연스럽다 (natural). Draw the line from 부끄럽다 and 창피하다: those are shyness/embarrassment about YOURSELF (blushing, shame), whereas 어색하다 is the awkwardness of an unfamiliar situation or relationship — no shame, just lack of ease; and 불편하다 is broader discomfort, while 어색하다 specifically flags social unfamiliarity. As a 하다 adjective it conjugates to 어색해요. English-speaker pitfall: don't use 어색하다 for personal embarrassment ('I was so embarrassed' is 창피했어요); reserve 어색하다 for that not-yet-comfortable-together or 'this looks unnatural' feeling.

usage: Nice to meet you / glad to see you
-(으)ㄴ attributive; news you're glad to hear
examples: It's so good to hear your voice.
여기서 고향 친구를 만나다니, 정말 반가워요!
To run into a friend from back home here — I'm truly delighted!
nuance: 반갑다 is the warm rush of gladness at meeting or seeing someone, and it powers Korea's everyday introduction 만나서 반가워요 ('nice to meet you'). It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: before an 아/어 ending the ㅂ becomes 우 and merges, so 반갑 + 아요 → 반가워요 (formal 반갑습니다, past 반가웠어요). Keep it firmly about PEOPLE (or news/voices tied to people) — you are glad to encounter someone — unlike 기쁘다, which is general happiness about any good thing (passing an exam, a sunny day). A handy contrast: 기쁘다 = happy in general; 반갑다 = specifically happy to see/meet someone; 즐겁다 = enjoyable/having a good time. usage: It itched, so I scratched it
examples: I got a mosquito bite and it's itching like crazy.
땀이 나고 가려우면 긁지 말고 시원한 물로 씻으세요.
If you sweat and itch, don't scratch — wash with cool water.
nuance: 가렵다 is the everyday word for a real, scratch-it itch — on skin, scalp, a healing wound, anywhere — the sensation that makes your hand reach to scratch (긁다). It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective, so the ㅂ becomes 우 before an 어 ending: 가렵 + 어요 → 가려워요 (past 가려웠어요). The core contrast is strength: 가렵다 is the stronger, want-to-scratch itch (mosquito bites, rashes, dry skin), while 간지럽다 is the lighter ticklish or fluttery feeling; native speakers reach for 가렵다 when it genuinely demands scratching. English-speaker pitfall: English 'itchy' covers both, so beginners overuse one — match the intensity, and crucially mark the body part with the subject particle 이/가 (등이 가려워요, 'my back itches'), not 을/를, because the body part is what HAS the itch, not an object being acted on. Note too that the verb you pair it with is 긁다 (scratch an itch), distinct from 깎다 (peel/shave) or 비비다 (rub).

english: to be a bother; annoying to do
usage: It's a hassle / I can't be bothered
I can't be bothered with anything
examples: Ugh, I can't be bothered to clean.
비 오는 날은 나가기 귀찮아서 그냥 집에 있어요.
On rainy days going out is a hassle, so I just stay home.
Cooking is nice, but washing up is such a drag.
nuance: 귀찮다 is the daily-life feeling that something is too much of a bother, not worth the effort — the 'ugh, I can't be bothered' reluctance to get up, cook, reply, or go out. It descends from a contraction of 귀하지 않다 ('not precious / not worth it'), which is why the ㅎ is nearly silent and 귀찮아요 is pronounced [귀차나요]. It pairs constantly with the -기 nominalizer to label a chore as a drag: 청소하기 귀찮아요, 나가기 귀찮아요 ('cleaning/going out is a hassle'). Draw the boundary from 피곤하다 and 짜증나다: 피곤하다 is physical tiredness (your body is worn out), 짜증나다 is irritation/annoyance at something, while 귀찮다 is specifically the can't-be-bothered, effort-averse feeling — you might feel 귀찮다 while perfectly rested. English-speaker pitfall: there's no clean one-word English match, so learners borrow 'annoying' and wrongly say 짜증나다; if the meaning is 'too much effort / I don't feel like it', the word is 귀찮다, often + a -기 chore.

usage: Are you having a hard time?
I earned it with great effort
examples: Living alone in a foreign place is hard.
요즘 회사 다니기 너무 힘들어서 그만둘까 생각 중이에요.
Lately work has been so tough I'm thinking of quitting.
nuance: 힘들다 literally takes 힘 (strength) + 들다 ('to take/cost'), i.e. 'it costs strength', and covers anything physically OR emotionally hard, tiring, or tough — a grueling shift, single-handed childcare, a rough stretch of life. With the -기 nominalizer it labels a hard task: 공부하기 힘들어요, 참기 힘들어요 ('studying/enduring is hard'). It is a ㄹ-stem word, so the ㄹ drops before endings beginning with ㄴ/ㅅ/ㅂ: honorific 힘드세요?, attributive 힘든 일, 힘듭니다 — not 힘들세요/힘들은. The crucial contrast is with 어렵다: 어렵다 is 'difficult to understand or solve' (a hard math problem, a tricky concept), whereas 힘들다 is 'taxing — tiring or emotionally draining'. A problem can be 어렵다 without being 힘들다, and a job can be 힘들다 (exhausting) yet not 어렵다 (intellectually hard). English-speaker pitfall: English 'hard' blurs both, so learners say 어렵다 for an exhausting day — if it drains your energy or spirit, it's 힘들어요, not 어려워요.

examples: I feel lonely when I'm alone.
I live apart from my family, so I'm lonely sometimes.
사람들 속에 있어도 마음이 외로울 때가 있어요.
Even surrounded by people, sometimes I feel lonely inside.
nuance: 외롭다 is the inner ache of loneliness — feeling alone, isolated, or cut off from people you love, even in a crowd. It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective, so the ㅂ becomes 우 before an 어 ending: 외롭 + 어요 → 외로워요 (past 외로웠어요), and its noun form 외로움 appears in the idiom 외로움을 타다 ('to be prone to loneliness'). The sharp contrast is with 심심하다: 심심하다 is surface boredom — nothing to do, easily cured by an activity — whereas 외롭다 is a deeper emotional emptiness that company, not just activity, would fill; 쓸쓸하다 is the close cousin, a wistful, forlorn loneliness (an empty house, autumn streets). English-speaker pitfall: English 'lonely' and 'bored' are sometimes used loosely/interchangeably, but Korean keeps them apart — if you just have nothing to do, say 심심해요; reserve 외로워요 for the heartfelt 'I miss having people around' feeling. Note it describes your emotional state, so the natural sentence is simply 외로워요, no object needed.
